subject: system-design
question: In Raft, what triggers a follower to start an election?
options: A client request
The leader reaching its log size limit
A configuration change
Not hearing from a leader within its randomized election timeout
explanation: Randomized timeouts reduce the chance of split votes.

subject: system-design
question: Why do Raft and Paxos clusters usually have an odd number of nodes?
options: Even sizes cannot elect a leader
Even sizes lose data
Odd sizes avoid network partitions
Adding a node to make an even count raises the majority size without tolerating any extra failures
explanation: Both 3 and 4 nodes tolerate one failure, so the fourth node adds cost without fault tolerance.

subject: system-design
question: In Raft, when is a log entry considered committed?
options: When the leader writes it to its own disk
When a client reads it back
When every follower acknowledges it
When the leader has replicated it to a majority of servers
explanation: Committing on majority replication means the entry survives any minority failure and will be seen by future leaders.

subject: system-design
question: How many total replicas are needed to tolerate f Byzantine (arbitrary) faults in a protocol such as PBFT?
options: 2f
explanation: Byzantine faults require 3f + 1 replicas; 2f + 1 is sufficient only for crash faults.

subject: system-design
question: What does the FLP impossibility result state?
options: In an asynchronous system, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination if even one process may crash
Consensus cannot tolerate any message loss at all
Consensus is impossible for clusters with more than three nodes
Consensus requires synchronized atomic clocks in every node
explanation: Practical protocols such as Raft and Paxos get around FLP with timeouts and partial synchrony assumptions, sacrificing guaranteed termination in some cases.

subject: system-design
question: How does Raft ensure that an elected leader has all committed entries?
options: The leader copies logs from every follower after election
A voter refuses candidates whose log is less up to date than its own
Committed entries are stored only on the leader
Clients resend all committed entries
explanation: Since committed entries are on a majority, any winning candidate must hold them.

subject: system-design
question: What problem do leader leases with fencing tokens address?
options: Slow disk writes on followers
A deposed leader that is paused or partitioned continuing to act as leader
Uneven sharding of keys
High read latency
explanation: Storage rejects requests carrying a fencing token lower than the latest one issued.

subject: system-design
question: What is the purpose of the term number in Raft?
options: It acts as a logical clock so stale leaders and messages can be detected and rejected
It sets the size of log segments on disk
It is the wall-clock time of the last heartbeat
It identifies the client that issued the request
explanation: Terms order leadership epochs, so a node that sees a higher term steps down and ignores lower-term messages.

subject: system-design
question: In Raft, a candidate becomes leader after receiving votes from:
options: Any single follower
Every node in the cluster
A majority of the cluster
Exactly half of the nodes plus the client
explanation: A majority quorum ensures at most one leader can be elected per term.
